text.p: Senior U.S. and Japanese trade negotiators resumed talks on Saturday in a race to settle differences on how to open up Japan's massive insurance market.
The two sides have set a deadline of Dec. 15 to resolve the trade dispute, and Japan's chief negotiator, Eisuke Sakakibara, told reporters in San Francisco that date remained Tokyo's target.
Sakakibara, director-general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, described the San Francisco talks thus far as "rough sailing."
Sakakibara said he wanted to set up a ministerial-level meeting, although he did not say when the proposed meeting would be held.

Senior U.S. trade negotiator Ira Shapiro said early on Saturday he did not know how long the session would last. "We don't have a schedule arranged," Shapiro said, adding he planned to leave for Washington on Saturday night.
Late on Friday, Shapiro told reporters major differences between the two sides remained. "We've had a good meeting, but differences are still significant," he said.
Shapiro and Sakakibara are leading the negotiations.

At issue is Japan's $382 billion domestic insurance market. Washington is pressing Japan to liberalize its primary insurance markets before a niche area called the "Third Sector," where U.S. firms have been dominant, is opened up to Japanese insurers.
The Third Sector includes areas such as personal accident, illness and nursing care, and stand-alone cancer policies.

The dispute has become a major trade irritant between the two countries. They had originally set a July 31 deadline to settle the dispute, but recently agreed to push the deadline to reach an agreement to Dec. 15.

The United States wants Japan to live up to a 1994 agreement that calls for deregulation of the primary sector dominated by big Japanese firms before deregulation of the so-called third sector of specialty insurance.

On Thursday, a U.S. trade official in Washington expressed doubt the dispute would be fully resolved in these talks. He said the "ball is substantially in Japan's court" because Tokyo removed a number of primary sector issues from the table during negotiations in September.
